passage: After the cremation of his father's closest friend, who had been fine at breakfast and gone by evening, Vishal, twenty-five, couldn't sleep. The village was quiet except for the dogs. He walked down to the river ghat where the pyre had burned, the ash still warm in the dark. His childhood friend Jeevan found him there. "You too?" Jeevan asked. Vishal nodded. "He was only fifty-eight. What's the point of all this, if it just stops?" His voice cracked. "I spend my days filling forms at the bank. Is that what I'm here for?" Jeevan sat beside him without answering. The river kept moving. After a long time, Vishal said, "I don't want to waste it." Jeevan said, "Then let's work out what not wasting it means."

qa.q: How old was the friend who died?
qa.a: Fifty-eight.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling as he sat by the river at night?
qa.a: He was shaken by how sudden death can be and felt afraid that his life might be meaningless or wasted.

qa.q: How did Jeevan help, and what could they do next?
qa.a: He stayed and listened instead of giving quick answers; next they could talk about what matters to each of them and try small changes.

qa.q: How might Jeevan be affected by the same death?
qa.a: He also couldn't sleep, which suggests he is facing the same questions about mortality and purpose.

grounding: Shows a young man in a village grappling with mortality and the meaning of his life after a sudden death.

passage: On the night of his twenty-sixth birthday in Hanoi, after the friends had gone home and the cake plates were stacked in the sink, Tuan sat on the balcony, staring at the motorbikes below. His partner Rania found him there. "You've been quiet since the candles." Tuan gave a small laugh. "I counted them. I've lived maybe a third of my life. What have I done? What will anyone remember?" He told her about his grandfather, who had seemed immortal until last year. Rania took his hand. She didn't tell him it was silly. "I think about it too," she said. "Sometimes it scares me into doing nothing. Sometimes it makes me want to call my mother." Tuan was silent. Then he picked up his phone and dialled his grandmother.

qa.q: Where did Tuan sit after his friends went home?
qa.a: On the balcony.

qa.q: What does Tuan's counting the candles reveal about his fear?
qa.a: He is afraid of time running out and worried his life may not add up to anything meaningful.

qa.q: How could Tuan turn this feeling into something useful?
qa.a: He could use it to reconnect with people and goals that matter, as he does by calling his grandmother.

qa.q: Why might Rania's reply help more than reassurance?
qa.a: She shared her own fears instead of dismissing his, making him feel less alone with them. 🤍

grounding: Shows a young man abroad confronting mortality and purpose on his birthday.

passage: At the palliative care centre where she volunteered on weekends, Nirmala, twenty-four, sat reading the newspaper aloud to an old man who could no longer see well. He fell asleep mid-article. She kept looking at his hands. On the bus home, her own heartbeat seemed loud. Everyone here knew their time was short. And hers? It was short too, just less visibly. That night she lay awake, feeling a cold weight in her chest. The next Saturday she told Nandini, the senior volunteer, about it in the corridor. Nandini nodded. "It happens to all of us here. The fear doesn't fully go. But it changes." "Into what?" Nirmala asked. Nandini smiled. "Into noticing things. Like how much he liked your voice reading."

qa.q: What did Nirmala read aloud to the old man?
qa.a: The newspaper.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling as she lay awake after her shift?
qa.a: Fear and dread, as she realised her own life was also limited, just less visibly than the patients' lives.

qa.q: Why was talking to Nandini a wise step?
qa.a: Sharing the dread with someone experienced helped her see the fear as normal and something that can change.

qa.q: How might the old man have experienced Nirmala's reading?
qa.a: He seemed comforted, falling asleep to her voice, which Nandini notices he liked.

grounding: Shows a young volunteer in a care setting grappling with mortality and what it means for her own life.

passage:
Baljeet,

It's past midnight and I can't sleep, so I'm writing instead of calling.

Since Nanaji's cremation last month, something has shifted. I keep thinking: one day it will be me on that pyre, and everyone I love too. I sat at my desk today, answering emails about quarterly targets, and suddenly none of it made sense. What is all this for?

It's not that I want to stop living. It's more like the floor turned out to be glass and I can see how far down it goes.

Nanaji spent forty years teaching village kids to read. I used to think that was small. Now I think he knew what his days were for, and I don't yet.

Can we walk by the canal on Sunday? I don't need answers. I just don't want to think about this alone.

Santosh

qa.q: Whose cremation does Santosh mention?
qa.a: Santosh mentions Nanaji's cremation last month.

qa.q: What is Santosh feeling when comparing the floor to glass?
qa.a: Santosh feels shaken and uneasy, suddenly aware of how fragile life is and unsure what those days are for.

qa.q: What did Santosh do that helps with feelings like these?
qa.a: Santosh reached out to a friend and asked to talk instead of carrying the thoughts alone; if the heaviness keeps going, speaking with a counsellor could also help.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Baljeet may feel concerned for a friend but also trusted, since Santosh chose to share something deep and asked simply for company.

grounding: A letter shows a young adult confronting mortality and questioning the purpose of their days after a grandparent's death.

passage:
"Farhan, you remember that night on the highway? The truck swerved, we stopped maybe a metre from the divider, and everyone got out laughing? I laughed too. But for weeks after that, I kept waking up at three. Not scared of trucks exactly. Scared that it could all just end, mid-sentence, and I'd have spent my life building spreadsheets for a company I don't even like.

I'd lie there and think, what's the point of any of it? Then in the morning I'd go to work like normal. That was the strangest part.

What helped, honestly, was my cousin. She didn't try to fix it. She said, 'Pranav, everyone meets this question at some point. You don't answer it in one night.' So now I'm just… living with it, and starting to ask what I'd want to be doing if I had ten years left."

qa.q: What time did Pranav keep waking up after the near-miss?
qa.a: Pranav kept waking up at three for weeks after the night on the highway.

qa.q: What was Pranav afraid of, if not trucks?
qa.a: Pranav was afraid that life could end suddenly, after being spent on work that did not matter.

qa.q: Why was Pranav's cousin's response helpful?

qa.q: What would change if Pranav had kept these thoughts private?
qa.a: Pranav might have stayed stuck in the night-time dread, without the reassurance that others face the same question and that it can be lived with.

grounding: A spoken account of a young adult grappling with mortality and meaning after a near accident.

passage:
I'm Nandini. I've shared a flat with Sonali for two years, and the month after her father's surgery she changed in ways I noticed but didn't fully understand.
She stopped watching shows with me. I'd find her on the balcony at eleven with a notebook, not writing much. Once she asked me, out of nowhere, whether I thought people in a hundred years would know we'd existed. I said probably not, and she nodded as if that was the answer she expected and didn't like.
I asked if she was okay. She said she wasn't sad exactly, just thinking about how short everything is. She said she'd talked to her cousin, and was going to see the counsellor at work. She did go.
By the end of the month she'd signed up to teach Saturday classes at the shelter near the market. She came back from the first one talking fast, hands moving.

qa.q: Where did Nandini find Sonali at eleven?
qa.a: She found her on the balcony with a notebook.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling in the month after her father's surgery?
qa.a: She seemed unsettled and heavy with thoughts about how short life is, uneasy rather than simply sad.

qa.q: What did Nandini and Sonali each do that was wise?
qa.a: Nandini asked directly if Sonali was okay, and Sonali talked to her cousin and went to see the counsellor at work.

qa.q: What might Sonali's hands moving after the first class suggest to Nandini?

passage:
After the funeral: Nazia, twenty-five, drove back from her cousin Bilal's funeral on a Thursday and couldn't sleep. He had been twenty-eight. At 2 a.m. she opened her work laptop, looked at a spreadsheet of shipping schedules and thought: is this what my one life is for?
Four days later: On an evening walk, she told her friend Vishal. “I'm not in danger or anything. I'm just scared of wasting it.”
Vishal listened, then said, “Scared how? What would not wasting it look like?”
She didn't know. That annoyed her.
Two weeks later: She sat with a notebook and wrote three questions: Who do I want near me? What do I want to have made? What do I want to have fixed? She didn't answer them all. But she emailed the literacy centre near her office and asked about weekend tutoring. Some nights were still hard. Fewer.

qa.q: How old was Nazia's cousin Bilal?
qa.a: He had been twenty-eight.

qa.q: What was Nazia afraid of after the funeral?
qa.a: She felt scared of wasting her one life, a dread about meaning rather than any danger to herself.

qa.q: Why was Vishal's question helpful?
qa.a: Asking what not wasting it would look like turned a vague dread into something Nazia could start to think through.

qa.q: What would change if Nazia had kept the fear to herself?
qa.a: She might have stayed stuck in sleepless worry without the push to name what she wanted and take a small step.

grounding: Over weeks a young woman grapples with mortality after a death and begins to shape a sense of purpose.

passage:
Dhruv, you asked if I was ever afraid of dying. Come, sit. Your Sharmila Nani will tell you.
I was twenty-five when my mother fell ill for the last time. I nursed her for eight months. At night, after she slept, I lay awake counting my own heartbeats. If she could go, so could I. So could everyone. What was any of it for?
One night she woke and saw my face. She didn't lecture me. She held my hand and asked me to read her the letters my father had written before they married. I read until dawn.
After she died, I kept thinking about those letters. Somebody had cared enough to write them, and somebody had kept them fifty years. That was an answer, of a kind.
I started writing too, to my sisters, to your mother. I still get afraid, Dhruv. But now I know what I'm doing while I'm here.

qa.q: How long did Sharmila nurse her mother?
qa.a: She nursed her for eight months.

qa.q: What was young Sharmila feeling as she lay awake at night?
qa.a: She felt frightened and lost, dreading death and wondering what anything was for.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Reading her father's old letters to her mother through the night showed her that caring and keeping connections gave life meaning.

qa.q: How might Sharmila's mother have felt when she saw her daughter's face that night?
qa.a: She probably felt tender and concerned, which is why she held her hand and asked for the letters instead of lecturing.

grounding: A grandmother recalls wrestling with fear of death at twenty-five and finding meaning in connection.

passage: Two days after Nani's funeral, Rukmini, twenty-five, and her cousin Farida sat on a bench at Itarsi junction. Their train back to Mumbai had been cancelled; the next one was in six hours. The platform was crowded and noisy. Rukmini stared at the tracks. "Nani was here, and now she's just... not. And one day that's me. And you." Farida didn't answer right away. "What's the point of all the deadlines and promotions," Rukmini went on, "if it just ends?" Her voice was flat. Farida bought two cups of chai and sat closer. "I think about it too," she said. "Maybe the point is what Nani did. Everyone at the funeral had a story about her feeding them." Rukmini held the cup with both hands. "I don't want to just rush through my life." "Then let's talk about how not to," Farida said. They talked until the train came.

qa.q: How long until the next train?
qa.a: Six hours.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling as she stared at the tracks?
qa.a: She felt a heavy dread and grief, confronting the reality that everyone, including herself, will die.

qa.q: What did Farida do that helped Rukmini face these questions?
qa.a: She listened, admitted she thought about it too, and pointed to the meaning in how Nani lived.

qa.q: How might Farida be feeling during the conversation?
qa.a: She is likely grieving too, but steady enough to stay close and keep talking.

grounding: After a grandmother's funeral, a young woman grapples with mortality and meaning while stranded at a station with her cousin.

passage: On the night Ujjwal turned twenty-six, the party in the Pune flat ended at two, and he couldn't sleep. His friend Kunal found him on the terrace, looking at the city lights. "Birthday blues?" Ujjwal was quiet for a long time. "Last month Rohan's bike accident. He's okay now, but for two days we didn't know. And I keep thinking, one day it won't be okay. For any of us." He rubbed his face. "I make slides for a living, Kunal. Is that it?" Kunal sat beside him. "It's a big thing to carry at two a.m." "I don't feel like I'm in danger. I just feel... lost." "Want to keep talking tomorrow, in daylight? Or see someone about it?" Ujjwal nodded. "Tomorrow. And maybe, yeah, someone." They sat until the sky began to grey.

qa.q: Whose bike accident did Ujjwal mention?
qa.a: Rohan's.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling on the terrace?
qa.a: He felt lost and full of dread about mortality and whether his life had meaning.

qa.q: What did Kunal do that helped?
qa.a: He sat with Ujjwal, named how heavy it was, and offered to talk the next day or help him see someone.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel finding his friend awake on the terrace?
qa.a: He may have felt worried at first, then relieved to hear Ujjwal wasn't in danger, and caring.

grounding: On his twenty-sixth birthday, a young man grapples with mortality and meaning after a friend's accident.

passage:
"Alka, the scan results take another hour."
"I know, Mridul. I heard."
"You're shaking."
"It's cold in here." She rubbed her arms. "Papa's always been fine. Always. And now we're in a hospital corridor waiting to hear if he's... not."
"The doctor said it could be nothing."
"I know. But sitting here, I keep thinking. One day it will be something. For him. For me."
Mridul took her hand.
"And then what was it all for? My job? The flat?"
"I don't know. Maybe the people."
Alka was quiet. "Papa spent his whole life teaching kids to read. That's his answer."
"What's yours?"
"I don't know yet." She squeezed his hand. "But I want to start looking."

qa.q: How much longer would the scan results take?
qa.a: Another hour.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling as she rubbed her arms?
qa.a: She felt frightened and full of dread about her father's health and her own mortality.

qa.q: What did Mridul do that supported Alka?
qa.a: He noticed she was shaking, took her hand and stayed with her questions instead of brushing them away.

qa.q: How does Alka's view of her father's life help her?
qa.a: Seeing that he found meaning in teaching children gives her a direction to start searching for her own purpose.

grounding: Waiting for a father's scan results, a young woman confronts mortality and questions of purpose.

passage:
The winter my grandfather died, I started lying awake doing sums. If I live to eighty, I have fifty-five winters left. Is that a lot? It didn't feel like a lot.
I'm Reena. I was twenty-five, with a decent job and a lot of plans, and suddenly none of them felt like enough. What was it all for, if it ended?
I told my friend Rashmi over chai. I expected her to laugh. She didn't. She said, "Everyone hits this wall. Some people climb it, some people build a house against it."
We talked for hours. I started writing down what I'd want people to say about me at the end. Not the job title. Kindness. Curiosity. Being there.
The dread still visits. But now it comes with a question: what matters today?

qa.q: What did Reena start doing while lying awake?
qa.a: Doing sums about how many winters were left.

qa.q: How did Reena feel after the grandfather died?
qa.a: Reena felt dread and a sense of emptiness, as if no plans were enough if everything ended.

qa.q: What helped Reena turn the dread into something useful?
qa.a: Talking honestly with Rashmi and writing down what really matters, like kindness and being there.

qa.q: How might Rashmi have felt hearing Reena's fears?
qa.a: Rashmi seemed understanding and calm, perhaps because she had faced the same wall.

grounding: A young adult reflects on grappling with mortality and redefining long-term purpose.

passage:
Counsellor's note, employee support programme
Sachin, 25, came in after a colleague his age died suddenly in a road accident. He said he had stopped sleeping well and kept asking himself what the point of his work was.
He was clear that he was not thinking of harming himself. He was frightened of dying, and more frightened of having lived without meaning.
His friend Tushar had suggested he come.
We did not try to answer the big questions. We talked about what gives his days weight: teaching his younger cousins maths, his grandmother's stories, the coding projects he actually enjoys.
He agreed to come back weekly for a month, and to tell Tushar or a family member if the fear grows heavier.

qa.q: What happened to Sachin's colleague?
qa.a: The colleague died suddenly in a road accident.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when he came in?
qa.a: He felt frightened of dying and afraid of living without meaning, and he wasn't sleeping well.

qa.q: What made the counsellor's approach helpful?
qa.a: The counsellor didn't force answers but explored what gives Sachin's days weight, and set up weekly support.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel knowing Sachin went to the counsellor?
qa.a: Tushar may feel relieved and glad his suggestion helped.

grounding: A counsellor records a young adult grappling with mortality and meaning after a sudden death.

passage:
Sunday, 1 a.m.
Can't sleep again. Abhinav's father's funeral today. He was only fifty-two.
Standing at the crematorium I kept thinking: everyone I love will go. So will I. And I spend my days making slides nobody reads.
It's not that I want to die. It's that I'm scared of it, and more scared of wasting the time.
Called Abhinav after. He said, "I keep thinking the same thing." We were quiet on the phone for ages.
Things I want to do: see Nani more. Finish the painting course. Ask for the NGO project at work.
Tomorrow I'll tell Maa I've been feeling like this. I don't want to carry it alone.
Minakshi

qa.a: Minakshi feels dread and fear about death and about wasting the time left.
